DM: Okay, so. Okay, so the sun is just beginning to sink in the sky as you ride along the road from Bas Udda north to Karawa, the Red Mesa looming on your left. It's been—it's May 23, so it's been about five days since you left the company of of Avaras and Pava at the stone house, about 10 days since you fled the orcs outside of Kharsan, and nearly a month since you left Karawa with Havdar to investigate rumors of orcs and the remains of the gnoll bands and whatever else might be lurking in the desert.

DM: The journey over the past five days from the stone house has been largely uneventful, although given the shadow attacks from a week ago, it's hard not to imagine you're seeing movement in the darkness every time you rest. And you've all gotten used to sleeping with the bright light of the drift globes as a constant evening companion. You're down to only three horses and Baxter, the shadows having taken two of them, and so it's been a hot, tiring journey as you've mostly had to walk alongside the animals, who are loaded with water and food for the desert trek.

DM: So now, as the long afternoon shadows cast by the Red Mesa begin to stretch across the desert, only a few hours from Karawa—the possibility of a fresh meal, maybe even a bath—you are anticipating your return.

Ah, many folks in town would like to speak with you, Candrosa in particular. If you have no urgent business—or will you come?
DM: So you ride with the messengers for for an hour into town. If you want to ask them any questions, you're certainly welcome to chat with them as you're traveling. Yeah, um, it was...
Kenzo: What's the news? The centaurs are still here, so as have there been any attacks or anything that eventful occurred in the past month?

DM: One of them, the—to—the one who hailed you is kind of riding ahead, sort of on point, and riding next you is a sort of middle-aged woman who's a—like, looks like an archer, tracker type. And, and she seems to be the one designated to sort of bring you the news. It's been—it's been pretty grim. There's been three attacks now from various creatures since you left. A few more have died in the battles. The—the danger of the blasted plain of the Nashtkar seems to be spilling over into Karawa more and more. And worse, a messenger from Samraat Karnas—the ruler of Dunmar, you'd know that. Remember way long ago you sent out a message to—to royal court? The messenger finally returned with news that the Samraat will not muster troops to defend Karawa. I'm saying, it is too far east. They will defend the Hara River, but no further.
DM: Has been concern in camp over this. As you might expect, Havdar is, well, uninterested in the Samraat's opinion. But others are not so sure we can remain here.
Kenzo: The river—the river at Tokra? Yeah also will defend that river and that's it.
Seeker: And that's—that's its—most, most of the population of Dunmar is west of that river, I guess.

DM: Most of the population, yeah. But there's that—but, you know, there's a—the population density on the land around here is much lower, but there's still quite a few people who live on the plains kind of north and west of of Karawa. And there's a handful of other villages that kind of around the Red Mesa where there's a number of oases. So it's not a it's not uninhabited, although many of those have fled west with the gnoll attacks.
Seeker: So these attacks on Karawa then all from the same type of creatures, do you know?

DM: Why, one was, yes. I was not here. We had not returned for most for most of these attacks. Supposedly giant vultures came hunting for live prey, which is unusual. And a swarm of ankhegs, I believe they're called—insect-like creatures that erupt from the earth and spit acid out of their jaws—attacked from the desert. And yes, another band of of the gnoll creatures as well, although some people, those who are here, say they were more dead than alive. And one of the centaurs come kind of comes in, rides over and says—um—

DM: Indeed, yes, they were hardly living at that point. Three had the flesh completely dropped off their body and seemed to be skeletons only. And yet they attacked with vigor, with arrows. It was not like anything I'd seen before. They seemed driven.
DM: In any case, Candrosa wishes to speak with you. Alesh also back in town, Havdar as well. I'm sure there are many who would discuss.
Kenzo: Indeed, we look forward to the council.

He had sort of a youthful, handsome face sort of, you know, black curly hair without no gray or anything is, you know, um—young-looking skin. He looks like he's aged maybe, you know, 10 years in the past, since you last saw him. It's like Barack Obama before presidency, Barack Obama after presidency.

DM: You know, something like that, um. And he says, I think... Well, I do not know what you've learned out in the desert. I think I think I have made a terrible mistake. But I would hear your news first, if you bring anything, of—anything that might be—that might bring some hope to the situation.
Kenzo: Well, there's news I think that's relevant to probably a larger council. On—been an eventful month.

Kenzo: But I'm glad we're we're able to meet in private as well, as we have learned about the Heart of Shakun. And we have learned—[garbled]. And I don't know, Candrosa, what you neglected to share with us before we departed, but it seems as though there's some critical information about—any information that you have about the Heart of Shakun and where we may be able to find it, that seems to be an incredibly important...
DM: Facet. Did you—how did you find such information? How did you come to learn of this thing?
DM: He looks shocked, not disbelieving, just like it sort of in awe.

Kenzo: I don't mean to to rush through parts of the story. I'm now an initiate of Bhishma. This is one of the events, nuts and bolts. Seeker nearly joined me the last minute had cold feet, understandably so. I mean you know dying is quite a price to pay, and—but, but yeah, I, you know Bhishma directly shared with me that while Shakun is still with them, the Heart is no longer, and that much of what we may be experiencing in terms of the lack of protection seems tied to its disappearance, which you seem to know something about and may not have shared.

DM: I will... I must say that news you bring brings me great relief. For I have been questioning in my mind whether Shakun would have me share this information with those not of our order. But if Bhishma herself told you, I need not worry of such things.

DM: I will not speak too much more of the story right now, for there is a traveler in town, a stoneborn from the mountains, who has come asking questions about—that touch on the same issue, about the failure of the barriers that have protected many beyond the borders of Dunmar as well as ourselves. And he has proven himself a defender of this town in several attacks, and so I would wait for him to share the full story.

DM: However, I wish to speak with you alone first, as I, I feel I owe you an apology. Especially you, Delwath. For you may remember a vision some time ago you thought was from a god. I am ashamed to admit that already at that time Shakun had left us. The Heart was gone, but I did not want anybody to know. And he sort of taps his staff and I have some control over dreams myself.

DM: I am sorry for the deception. And I am sorry I did not trust you earlier, but there are some things... Well, it is hard to explain. The secrets of Shakun, they are... It is difficult to even speak of them. And not—I say difficult to speak of them because I don't wish to, or I, you know, don't trust you, or don't wish to share widely this information. I mean difficult to speak of them literally.

DM: And so I will try as best as I can tell you the story. In any case, I'm sorry did not try to give you more information earlier. Every death since then has been on my conscience, and when the four of you first fought off those animal attacks on town, I wonder what may have gone differently if I had come clean then. And perhaps some deaths could have been averted.

DM: He sort of pauses for a moment. Somehow you can help, and maybe too, I hope, somehow I can help you. Because I know many of you came to town originally with questions about other things and were drawn into these mysteries, perhaps not entirely—not, not entirely as the first choice of things you would have done. And even though I can't—I can't change what's happened, I hope somehow we can make the future better.

Seeker: We hope so too, and thank you for sharing these difficult things to share, such as they are. It does seem that worry can age a person, and you, you seem to be aged with worry. But it does not usually seem to be the case that worries can age a temple. It seems to me, however, that this temple that we're in is showing much greater signs of wear, perhaps the wear you might see over centuries, just in the weeks that we've been gone. I wonder if you've noticed this.

DM: Indeed. How could I not? This perhaps is a secret that is easier to speak of, and that I will share with you. So you have seen some of the healing concoctions that we make from the earth of this mesa.
Seeker: Yes, we've used and benefited from them greatly.

DM: Inside the—deep in the temple, below the temple—there is a—there is a chamber, a cave where those concoctions grow. The stone itself grows as plants and renews itself, and we harvest them, the fruits of the stone plants, and use them to make these powders and ointments.
Seeker: Plants—do—is there anything in dwarven lore of this kind of thing?

DM: No. Dwarves are not—but also dwarves are not so, ah. You know, you're much more interested in, you know dwarves and what they can do, right? Not the coaxing the stone to—to grow, but but actually what it does. I mean, it does remind you of you know caves, and there are you know, obviously, like stalactites, stalagmites. Many cave formations do grow over time.
Seeker: I would love to see these red mud farms.
DM: Perhaps at some more relaxed moment, I would be honored to give you a tour. But to finish the important points: they have stopped growing.

DM: About six weeks ago. Maybe a little longer ago. And now, but I think they have been slowing, and perhaps it was actually when Shakun's Heart was lost that they—that's the energy that lets them grow disappeared. And I am not a—I'm not a scholar of these things, but somehow it seems to me there must be a connection between the way that mesa looks and the growing stone.
Seeker: Perhaps the temple itself is made of this stone.

DM: I would not begin to know how to understand or test such a thing. But yes, it could be, very well. That mesa itself seems to renew itself a fresh every year, whenever there is, you know the winds weather it, the sands sandstorms blow. It never... It grows again. Yes, maybe, maybe there is some connection.

Kenzo: Candrosa, before we meet with others to hear more: you have betrayed our trust. We've suffered and fought and killed horrible things and dealt with some pretty terrible situations, and I think your lack of forthcomingness about the whole context of the danger that we were subjecting ourselves to is not an easy slight to forgive, honestly.

Kenzo: Before we meet with the others, I don't know if there's anything else you want to share. I know before we left most recently, it seemed as though there was something you wanted to share with us, but you felt pains and ultimately did not share on—but if there's anything that you want to to explain further to us before we meet with others, that may be appreciated. I certainly have empathy for your situation and understand that there's been some very traumatic events that have unfolded here as well. But I think on our—what has been such a primary motivator of our journeys has been trying to understand what the hell is going on, and not having key pieces of insight into this as we've traveled has been—has been detrimental to our cause.

DM: I cannot argue against anything you say, Kenzo. I—I am not the person who should have been the speaker of Shakun in these times. I was... I don't know what to say. I was—I was trained and and expecting a very different role: bringing people together, maintaining the bonds of community, preaching and healing. Not facing the destruction of everything I had, everything that was my life for the past 35 years. I have no excuse.
Kenzo: What did you neglect to tell us? What were you trying to tell us before we left that you did not tell us—the...?
DM: That Shakun's Heart was missing.
Seeker: And we suspected that something like that would be the case. But it's still hard to understand why you might need to hide that fact.

DM: Initiates? The first non-initiates ever who are aware of the existence of this artifact. And even now I try to explain what it does, and I can form the words and I tried to speak them and nothing comes out. That—the power of this thing is not so simple to understand or speak of. The gods work in mysterious ways, Shakun most of all.
Kenzo: Who else knows that the Heart is missing?
DM: I suspect Tharandros has his suspicions, although whether he knows, I have not spoken to him of the such artifact. If he knows this, he must know that from the centaur leader.
Seeker: And did did Kenzo actually see an image, I'm trying to remember, of the Heart?

DM: Yeah, it was like a red ochre stone that wasn't—didn't have a solid form that you could like visualize. It was like changing and pulsing and growing and shrinking, but it reminded you of the stone of the Red Mesa.

Delwath: Heart. Maybe what is keeping the mesa be growing, although it's deteriorated today. Was it just recently that it's really deteriorated a lot, whereas it that it's more noticeable, but it's...?
DM: It's—it's actually a—Seeker, why don't you make a Intelligence check?
Wellby: Did he, did he already tell us where physically the Heart resides now? What is that?
Kenzo: He wants to tell us that in the presence of the stoneborn in greater detail.

DM: So yeah, Seeker—Seeker is pretty experienced with stone and it's—all its forms of weathering and construction, and I think, Seeker, what you would infer from this is that, like structural weaknesses had probably been building up for a while, and something...

DM: Part of one of these attacks, or just like you know one rock cracks and that triggers—and stuff. Okay. So it's hard to say exactly how it's—it seems like it's an accelerating process of decay, but not something that just started three weeks ago. It's probably been going on for a while and has just gotten more noticeable. Maybe not as far back as when you first came to Karawa, like then there was—you had spent some time examining the mesa and there was nothing—nothing obvious. But perhaps by the time you returned after the first gnoll attack, when the village was ruined, you just passed off any damage that accumulated as just the after effects of the battle.
Seeker: But from the start, I noticed that it was older than the surrounding rock, paradoxically.

DM: Yes, exactly. Which probably contributes to your suspicion that the mesa is somehow the same stone as whatever's in this cavern, is growing out from the cavern or something, but it stopped growing at some point in the past and damage is now becoming more obvious.

Seeker: So, well, yeah, the whole thing is still a little weird. It's as though it has accelerated formation compared to normal stone, or just like magic formation, but then also the reverse of that: accelerated aging.
DM: It's like all the aging that was—hasn't happened, that never happened because it was magically growing, is suddenly happening to it, right?

Kenzo: Well, Candrosa said before we meet with the others, I mean that maybe we also have some more questions as we—we've gone and learn more. What do you know about—what do you know about the the wizard, the mage Rai?
DM: Rai? Well, I've been—he was a hero in the Great War, was he not?

Kenzo: He was. But as we learned in our our travels, as we engage more with the initiates the Bhishma, and there may have been—and [garbled]—a collaboration, I suppose, between some of the initiates and Rai to potentially try to close a portal. It's in—some, something that was—that may have some relationship to the unfolding of these beasts that are are now these strange beast that are now attacking Karawa and Dunmar. So we're trying to learn more about history.
DM: As I said, I am not a scholar. I—I sat through my studies of history and religion like the next person, but I can't say much of it has sunk in.
Kenzo: Well it's it's just to be clear again, no one else knows? Does anybody in town even know about the existence of the Heart of Shakun?
Kenzo: Only the initiates when—and who else knows that it's gone, other than you? And...
DM: I will, I will tell that story, but I would prefer not to tell it twice. So let us speak with a stoneborn first.
Kenzo: And why do you trust the stoneborn—the stoneborn?

DM: He... There is a magic about him, something of the mountains. He came from the north seeking answers to—well, the barriers that have protected Dunmar have also protected many of those beyond our borders. The stoneborn, the dwarves of the Yuvanti, many others who have been... Even Chardon have not seen the evils of the Blasted Plains cross these lands and reach their hearths. This has obviously ceased to function.

DM: And as such, enraged beasts full of bloodlust and other things that he tells me have have come to his people as well. And to be honest, I was afraid of repeating the mistakes I made with another coming to help and seek answers. Um, he—he aided us in battle. He has tried to heal some of my exhaustion and and trouble. When I spoke with him, there was a—there was something of the mountains about him. And he's been in town for almost two weeks now, and I've had the chance to converse with him. If I—if I trust you, I will trust him. He has the same interests at heart.

DM: Maybe. Like, not totally convinced, but I appreciate the effort.
Wellby: Wellby shakes his head. Surely I have no relationship with Shakun whatsoever at all, can't have more faith in their judgment than you. And I'll laugh and leave it at that.

interactions.title: The missing Heart and the Oracle’s journey
lines: DM: Um, so you—as you walk back through—through camp, you get the sense that, like a number of the centaurs are sort of familiar with with Drikod, and a few wave and say hi and—as he walks past it until you come back to the temple. DM: As I've told these friends, Drikod, there are some things that—about the story I'm going to tell that are hard to speak. Not—not that I'm unwilling to speak—that are literally hard to speak because of the magic of Shakun and the mystai initiation. And so, you have more questions when the story is over, perhaps it may be possible to show you what I mean. But we can discuss that once you know more. And he takes a deep breath and he kind of says a brief prayer to Shakun. Puts a staff—leans a staff down and kind of sits with his hands on the table.

DM: I am speaking this story to you because I believe that only—that somehow, together, if we can find a way going forward, we may be able to solve this crisis. And I—I have no choice but to put my faith in you, and I am glad to do so. But this story is not known to anyone outside this room. Some of the details and information are known to other initiates of the mystai of Shakun, but none are known to non-initiates.

DM: And I would ask you to be cautious in how you repeat these stories. Our story begins with Shakun's Heart. So many of you have heard of this. This is a... And he's like struggling to speak. I think all I can really say is, it is a piece of Shakun's power. It is—it is—to explain it, it is not simply a piece of Shakun's power. It is a—a piece of her.

DM: It amplifies her power. It amplifies divine magic in this world, and it gives strength to the community of mystai that protects the land. It has been part of Dunmari history for many, many generations, sitting here in this place at what was once the heart of Dunmar, now left as the eastern edge of this land. And just as her brother Kotana gave his body and mind to build this country, Shakun gave her heart to protect that.

DM: Two and a half years ago—and before I go on, let me tell you another secret, which is easier to speak of. I am the speaker of Shakun. But there is another one in whom the power of Shakun lives, one who is born every generation with Shakun's essence in them: the Supreme Oracle. In this generation, her name is Cintra.

DM: Two and a half years ago, she had a daughter. A child late in life, a blessing to her and all of us. From a very young age she seemed as one blessed by Shakun's favor. Before she could even speak, she could shape the earth around her and paint colors in the desert sand.

DM: But then, not when she was not yet two—maybe seven months ago now, six months ago now—she took ill, slowly wasting away, not eating, growing frailer. We all prayed. And while I had misgivings in my heart that, again, I did not speak, Cintra was convinced that Shakun was speaking to her and that her daughter would be a great oracle, and to heal her she needed to take her and Shakun's Heart south beyond the mesa to a place called Shakun's Wellspring, a sacred grove hidden on the southern end of the Red Mesa.

DM: Ah, yes, the first one. Um—Shakun's Wellspring is a sacred grove—I said that already, um. I should have spoken. I should have said something then, but I told her to go. That was early February. Neither her nor her daughter has returned since then, and the Heart has not been seen. We thought she'd be gone maybe two weeks, three at most. Some knew, many knew of her travels, highest level of initiates anyway. She took two companions with her, although she is the strongest of us. Some time ago now, early March, I asked some more acolytes to go investigate. They never returned. And soon after, the first hyena attacked Karawa.

DM: And things went downhill from there. Another group of our strongest warriors remaining left after the gnoll attack—I'm sorry, before the gnoll attack—and they again have not returned. I have tried, for my morale as much as anything, to keep up appearances since we lost the Heart. But without that, my magic is weak. And more than my magic, the community cannot do what it needs to do to keep us safe. I hesitate. I hesitate to ask you to travel where many others have gone and died.

DM: And part of my hesitation before was fearing that whether I speak or stay silent, I will send somebody to their death. But... And I cannot explain how Shakun's Heart powers the protection that guards our borders. I—the words to speak the nature of this magic or—I'm prevented from doing so. I—I can show you, if you desire.
DM: But whether you wish to see the magic of the Heart or not, I would ask you if you would travel south and tried to find Cintra and Shakun's Heart.
Seeker: Can I just review for a second? So Cintra is the Supreme Oracle of the Shakun mystics, yep, and so someone perhaps like alongside Candrosa on the org chart, or even above?

DM: Well, yeah, you get the sense that it's sort of like she's not on the org chart like she's—literally the soul of Shakun somehow empowers her and is sort of nowhere. Cintra—or sorry, Candrosa—is formally the head of the organization of the monastery, of the whole temple and the mystai and everything. But Cintra just kind of floats around and sometimes speaks with her voice in this, like, that—that's what's happening, and then everybody listens to her. Sometimes it's just an ordinary woman. And maybe not ordinary, but clearly very magical.
Seeker: About the story, but so and she has a daughter who fell...
DM: A daughter who fell sick.
Seeker: And then she thought she could heal the daughter using the Heart, but I had to go to this sacred grove, yes?
Kenzo: Wait, is the daughter the Heart, or is the daughter—Heart a physical object?
DM: The Heart's a physical object. The daughter was just a person who can do magic.
Seeker: Will be the next Supreme Oracle and infuriatingly powerful.
Kenzo: Yes, right. And so they took this to Heart with them. Yes, so...
DM: Like, like on the other end, the southern end of the mesa.
Wellby: Go get her, be back tomorrow.
Seeker: No, I'm personally not very experienced with small children, but perhaps someone else in the party is.
Wellby: I'm sure that she and I will see eye to eye.
Seeker: And I perhaps share with her some of those interests and skills in shaping and coloring stone. Do...
Delwath: Do we know how old is the, this is the daughter, do we know how old she is?

DM: She's probably like—like three now, if she's alive. I mean, nobody knows if she's alive. She was dying of some wasting disease, and went to be healed and never came back. So big question mark there.
Wellby: Who knows? There's someone south of here who does favors in return for a terrible price, right?
Kenzo: It was just like so frustrated like just so like—like, what? When did we first show up here? How many months ago is it?
Kenzo: It was just like they—Candrosa, that...
Seeker: People. People want to do amazing things to protect and grow their own children.

Kenzo: That Candrosa, like four months. Yeah, traveling hundreds of miles, the desert through fighting terrible beasts, uncovering horrible secrets. I mean we haven't—we still have to share with you some of what we what we learned in the lands east of here, but...

Kenzo: The protection of Dunmar through Shakun and the Heart, these feel like primary issues of critical importance that, if solved first, could have potentially prevented or help to address so many the urgent issues. Why have the centaurs not been rallied to this cause? Why have we not been talking about this the moment that we arrived? This is just what we've been wandering around the desert for hundreds of miles for.

Kenzo: Sorry if I'm a little agitated right now, but you're talking to us after you know being gone ourselves for a month and having to learn about the the the disappearance of the Heart from the Bhishma directly. I mean, I'm just a little frustrated, and [garbled].
Wellby: Wellby was saying, And don't get us wrong, all of that has been...

DM: This secret perhaps has outlived its usefulness.

DM: Yes, the—the Wellspring. It's at the southern edge of the of the mesa.
Delwath: That's like—this is the mesa, right? This?

DM: Well, it's not precisely to scale, but yes. It's like it's like 30 to 50 miles, roughly. It's hard to—yeah, maybe like maybe like 40 miles or something, somewhere in that range. It is a—many places around this mesa are sacred to Shakun and have been kept secret and protected for many generations. The—the Wellspring is a hidden grove around a pool that can be reached through steps that lead down into a narrow slot canyon, which continues to the far southern edge of the mesa, where a enormous bowl is open to the sky, maybe 700, 800 feet across. And in the center of that opening in this canyon is this grove.
Seeker: So it's reached by going over the top of the mesa?
DM: Yeah, over the top of the mesa, find the stairs, go down the stairs, go through the canyon. Hmm, or, you know, scale down a...

DM: I—there has much that has always been secrets about Shakun and the places and things associated with her. I do know not—I do not know what the consequences will be of revealing such information. I suspect they will not be none. But I no longer trust my judgment in any of this.
Kenzo: So, Candrosa, do you have any speculations on what may have befallen Cintra, the child, the Heart?

DM: I suspect Cintra and the child are dead. And the Heart, I hope, remains at the Wellspring, protected somehow by Shakun's magic but with no means of returning it to where it belongs. That is what I hope.
Kenzo: And it belongs here in the mesa? There's a home for it here?
Seeker: Who is the father of the child?
DM: I do not know. Cintra would not say. But such is not atypical for the oracles. It...

Seeker: I think we'd like to see.

DM: It is not simple. The only way to see is to experience part of the—the ritual that we use to initiate new members into the order. It will take some time to prepare. But tomorrow evening, I could be ready.
Drikod: Can we afford to wait one more day?
Seeker: It could make all the difference.
DM: It's been—it's been four months since Cintra left. I think the delay—the blame for delay is mine.

Delwath: When all the bad stuff started happening.

DM: Possibly, yes. The first animal attack that—so in Karawa, Delwath, when you were in Karawa, the first hyena attack was—was in early March, so roughly three weeks after Cintra left. And similarly your, you know other experiences in town of—things all happened after the beginning of February. In terms of like larger bad things having to do with this stuff out in the desert, yeah that you are suspecting like when you—you are suspecting was like nine to 12 months ago. The timeline was a little uncertain, so it does not seem to entirely line up with—with this being the cause of bad stuff in the desert.
Delwath: Drikod, what—when did bad things coming to your village?

Drikod: I have sensed unsettling things in my travels in the wilderness, in the mountains, for a while. I'm—over a decade ago, decades ago, things have been unsettled but slight in the mountains. But it's getting more and more in the past 12 months. And the unsettling feelings I have felt in the mountains and my travels, coupled with the rumors that have been even making it into these rural, isolated villages—how—the elders have sent me down to figure what is up. So it's escalating, but it does predate the very poor decisions of this priest.
Delwath: Well, Candrosa, what— have you told the centaurs anything?

DM: I have not told them any of these secrets. I have told them—that they are aware that our magic is failing. I've told them little beyond acknowledging that the magic has failed and I'm hoping for a solution.

Kenzo: Yeah. You may find yourself in another political situation with the centaurs also not being aware of the true nature of the problem. They are here presumably until the Heart is returned. They are, they are sacrificing of themselves as well. Do you know anything about the nature of the dangers we may face? Should we—should we marshal troops? Should we bring more horsemen? Should we have the centaurs join us, we have any—do you know if this requires—if this mission requires stealth? Does it require might?
DM: There is little I know for certain. There are few now left among the mystai who have any real power. Most of our—most of us who did have power have already gone and failed on this mission.
Delwath: Scout, I mean if, when it's 30 miles, you said?
DM: Like, probably 40. It's between 30 and 50. I...
Delwath: And he's proposing this ritual...

DM: Tomorrow—no, sorry, no, it's evening. He's proposing it tomorrow night, yeah. But it's still the same day you got into town, like you've basically done nothing, haven't even set up camp or checked on your belongings or anything.
DM: But it's—ah, yes, so you know I mean he's happy to delay...
DM: Ceremony, if you want, right? I mean...
Kenzo: I think that's a good rest and resupply. Have a hot meal.

DM: You know, he's—like, you really get the sense he doesn't—he really doesn't think anybody's alive or anybody's there. He thinks this is a scouting/stealth mission. And he is nervous about breaking with—I mean, clearly he's already stretched tradition to tell you. But you're all outsiders, and trust you not to tell anybody. He—he definitely—now if you suggest that, he's like enough unsettled with his own judgment he'll go along with that. But he's definitely nervous that it's not that there's something might happen if the secret is breached. And, you know, what...?
Delwath: Are there any examples in Dunmari history of secrets being...?

DM: Yes, anybody—anybody who wants to. Um, so, I mean, there are—so there's not much that is, you know obvious in Dunmari history that's like, here, there was a secret that a bunch of people said, and here's this bad thing that's directly attributable to that secret. But you know Kenzo in particular, as you as you kind of think about it, you know, given your you know your study and your connection to—to the monastery, or to Dunmar, right? Um, you know, there's definitely like there's this strand of kind of mystical history that runs through the Dunmari tradition, and you know, particularly around, you know, how the rulers are chosen, for example, like, for a long time this was kind of a secret of the Lakan monastery, Laka being another one of the Dunmari god's. Drikod probably would know the names of the gods at least um. And...

DM: But that—that failed. And, and when that sort of part of the Lakan tradition sort of became public and got out and that was what led to eventually um you know, a series of rulers who pushed Dunmar to expand its borders and stretch south and led to the end of that dynasty, and—and the sort of breaking of that line of—of—of rulers. And, you know kind of at the end of that dynasty there was you know they were attacking they were like pushing into Drankor and doing some you know moving south, and suffered like lost a bunch of battles badly and so that's the closest parallel you can think of, where kind of secret knowledge became unsecret knowledge, and it—not necessarily a great precedent in terms of—now, whether this is that significant like it's pretty unclear, but...
Delwath: Can. I also think we should tell the centaurs about the Heart.
Kenzo: I'm feeling that as well, but I'm also feeling like that's Candrosa's political mistake, not ours. It's like, I mean. I got it awesome.
Wellby: They'll just say—are we still with Candrosa? Yeah—said of Candrosa, “Candrosa, tell Tharandros.”
Delwath: One. Go ahead. I'm— Tharandros knows something is missing. I think if you are—I think you must share it. And if...

Delwath: You said earlier you do not trust your judgment. I think if you will not—that was trying to think of Delwath-y words, but I'm trying to think of a playoff. I—he's mostly forceful, but... If you will not... I do not think it is safe for this secret to be kept. Centaurs are trustworthy. They will not share with others of Dunmari.

Kenzo: You risked deeply betraying their trust and the lives and the blood that's already been shed if—that—you did—they do not understand the full picture. And they already know that Delwath said, they know something is wrong and know something is missing, and they've committed to stay here until the hearts return, even though they don't know exactly that it is the Heart that needs to be returned.
Wellby: Don't keep making the same mistake.

DM: He looks around at all of you, and then he looks specifically at Drikod and he says, “You're right. If I'm willing to trust one stranger from the north, I should trust another stranger from the north.” You're muted.
DM: That's like the west, more or less. And he says, “Okay. I will—I will tell them tell them tonight.”
Seeker: Have one other question. With ill intent got a hold of this Heart, in addition to the harm of keeping it from Shakun in the temple, could they make use of it to their own ends?
DM: Do not know. Perhaps. The Heart is—it is... It is called a heart, but that is not a metaphor. And yes, somebody could do great harm with this thing.

Delwath: Candrosa, would you have any way of knowing if this secret was known by others, this fact of the Heart away, perhaps? There are there are treasure seekers on the plain, from Chardon and much darker places. They be seeking this?
DM: Part of the point of secrecy is to prevent such things. But I do not know. I cannot say for sure that the secret is not known. As I said, I'm not a scholar.
Delwath: And you, through the dreaming?
DM: Perhaps. Perhaps I should try, yes.
Delwath: Perhaps we should leave you to your errands, Candrosa. Been a long day for us, and a long travel. And Delwath looks at the rest of us. Anybody else?
DM: I will speak with Tharandros and pray and prepare. And send a message if you change your mind. Otherwise I will expect you tomorrow around sunset.

interactions.title: The incomplete initiation and shared vision
lines: DM: The following evening, you return to the temple, and Candrosa is there along with a couple other mystai of Shakun, they are wearing—they are both wearing—um—all of them are wearing these ochre robes. Candrosa is carrying his staff, but the other three mystai are you know carrying nothing, just just the robes. And, and Candrosa says to you as you approach...

DM: As part of our usual initiation into the mysteries of the goddess Shakun, we are exposed, we are become in some real way... And he sort of stops. I—I need to show you. This will not be the—this is not the full initiation, because the full initiation into the mystai is not possible without the Heart. Hope maybe you can understand how its absence has affected us. I think without it, maybe it is hard even for me to think straight, having so long been in the presence of its magic. And while I cannot perform the full ritual for you, I can do enough to show you to show you the magic of the Heart, even its absence. And hopefully then you will see how it works and why it is important.

DM: And I should warn you: part of the magic of this place, part of the ritual of—of the initiation, is tying us mystai together in a shared experience of Dunmar, by sharing all our experiences together of this place we have called home for generations. None of you grew up in this land, and I do not know exactly what will happen, as—for this part of the ritual. I can promise no harm will come to you. I do not know what you will see. Are you prepared to go forward?

DM: And he holds out—he has like a bunch of um—sort of pale gray robes, and he he looks at Wellby and at Drikod, it's like—and Seeker, actually—is like, I—I've done what I could. And he asks you to change into these robes. And then he takes this red ochre stone and paints like a crescent on each of your foreheads. And then he leads you into the temple.

DM: So as he leads you into the temple, he takes you through into the sort of main hall of the temple, the sort of central sacred space, and he says, “Normally initiates would be blindfolded as they enter, and all would be dark. And they would—the first thing they would see as they enter the under the temple would be the Heart of Shakun. Because the Heart is gone, and because this not is not an initiation ritual, because I've already told you our secrets, I will escort you unblindfolded through the temple.”

DM: And he leads you. So be—so there's where you are right now, where you sort of initially walk in his—you know, his—you sort of pass through. You're sort of in this shrine/temple area. It's a big room stretching back into the into the center of the—of the mesa, and there's light shining from like big—these big columns that light, let light in on the second floor. But on three sides, you know it's inside the mesa, so there's only windows on one side. And on the far wall there are like two archways that lead down into the darkness. And he lights a torch, which which burns with a blue flame.

DM: And he takes you down one of these corridors into another room like a sort of almost like an indoor cloisters in some sort of weird sense, that has these large skylights cut into them—into the ceiling like going up hundreds of feet, these shafts into the to the earth. And now, because it's evening, there's only a sort of pale reddish light shining, and everything seems to be glowing slightly with this reddish light. And there's two—one sort of chamb—one passageway that exits leading up, one passage that exits leading down. He points towards the one leading down and says, “Seeker, that is the rock garden. Someday perhaps we'll have time to explore it together and think about its mysteries.”
Seeker: I look forward to that day.

DM: And he leads you forward past the cloisters, going down again um—into a chamber that is dark, a cave glowing only with a faint blue light from four torches lit again around the walls that are casting blue light everywhere. Everything is gray and shadow, as if you're watching the world through a thin, dark curtain, like a veil that sort of preventing you from seeing clearly. And you seem to be floating above a tumbled scrub land of rock and grass and low hills, and you can sense your companions with you, but you can't see them. You can just feel their presence next to you. The ground is moving beneath you, but you don't feel a sense of movement. It's as if you're stationary and the ground is scrolling. DM: The land is moving quicker now, a blur almost, as if you are—as if it's like somebody sped up the film. And you begin to drift higher and higher, and you can see across the entire sweep of Dunmar as if you're floating far up in the sky. You can see a river glittering in the distance, tall mountains rising out of the plains to the north, open fields below, tall grass blowing in the wind. Everything seems like you know child's toys laid out below you, and you see the rain falling, a summer thunderstorm washing the earth clean. And as you begin to fall back towards the earth, the image changes.

DM: And you see the faint flicker of a vast forest of unimaginable trees superimposed on the land, growing above and as part of the plains, stretching as far as you can see, reaching the mountains. Still in shadow, still through a veil, but every now and then pierced by lights, and you can hear the sound of singing in a strange language. Flickering trees slow, and they steady for a moment, almost as if you're paused above the world, and you can see clearly this forest of trees stretching. Until time pauses. And with a flash, ash and fire spreads across the land, and everything is red with the flame. You see nothing but ash and dead trees across the land. You see burning, fighting, the smell of blood and death, until the image fades again.

DM: And you drift closer, and you're looking at a huge city that's spreading out below you, growing, stretching, covering all that you can see. An impossible city, which then melts and begins to ooze across the land like red blood, until a light cuts across it, water falling, washing it clean.

DM: And as the land is cleansed, you're disoriented for a moment because you are the rain, flowing down the river into an ocean. Somehow both yourselves, but also part of the water. Almost as if your your individual identity is gone, and you're catching impressions from the water around you that both are yours and not yours: the pungent smell of blood and war, the taste of mushroom and lamb stew. The acid, ashy taste of some bitter, polluted smoke in the air. The sound of gulls, the smell of salt in the air. Clean, crisp, cold taste of water from a high mountain stream.

DM: Until just as suddenly you evaporate into the sky, a cloud drifting over the land, growing as you rise in the hot air over the dry plains below, until you burst. And still everything is faint and seen through a veil, but now it feels more like a fine mist than a shadow. And as you're falling, the earth rises up to meet you, eager for the life you bring, and as you soak into the ground, everything's dark and earthy around you.

DM: And then suddenly you feel like you're being stretched in five different directions, almost like you're being pulled apart, until you burst forth, images flashing. Seeing yourself turning the corner on a narrow track high in the mountains, watching small trails of smoke rising in the distance from the cook fires of the small village. And feeling the anticipation of hearing again the sounds of hammers against stone, the soft patter of young feet running over the earth, the background murmur of life. And as you walk forward approaching the village, you take a step and are falling through the mountains, through the stone, emerging on an enormous white fur rug by a fireplace, looking up at a vaulted ceiling covered in complex patterns of tile.

DM: Until you turn in anticipation as you hear the distant roaring of water growing louder, and then watch as water starts cascading down the facade of the building you are in, a roaring current. And as you are enveloped by the joy of this sight, you notice the water is driving a number of small stone and glass automata, which starts to move. And you're drawn into them, zoom in closer as they begin to come to life. And you are drawn into one of them, a glowing crystal lantern, as your vision pulls out, and you can see now that this lantern is sitting on a beautiful and intricately carved mantel. It seems ancient, and as your gaze falls upon it, you feel a sense of loss and melancholy as you stare at the light.

DM: And as you focus on the light, it becomes the sun setting behind you as you're on a ship at sea, cutting through green waters, watching the waves, the wind in the sails, as you leave the port. Watching the sun set behind you on the shore, a sense of happiness and contentment at setting off for somewhere new. And as the sun sets, the image fades into the night sky full of stars, clear and bright, and a sense of calm washes over you. As for a moment you feel a sense of profound peace, and everything slows and pauses.

DM: And your vision clears for a moment, and you see a great empty cavern, vast but dark, the only light coming coming from shimmering crystals surrounding seven carved thrones of stone, an intricate design etched on the rocks below. A strange mineral-y taste in your mouth, almost like placing your tongue against the vein of some metal in an ancient rock face. And as you rushed towards the floor and crashed through it, for the briefest of briefest of moments, you can see everything.

DM: You can see the world below you, lines of energy twisting across it, points of thought super imposed too complex to understand. But for a moment you feel as if everything is clear, and you can see people. You can see the mystai of Shakun. From each one a light stretches into a web, and that web stretches together into a complex interweave of energy that reaches out across Dunmar and stretches for the border and piles up. But as you watch this web, you can see that there are holes in it. You can see that it's tearing. It's beginning to pull apart. And you follow these strands, and you can see that this energy is coming both from here, from Dunmar, and from elsewhere.

DM: And it's tied together into this web of power, shifting and shimmering with the thoughts of the people whose dedication supports that. But at the center, where there should be energy, where there should be light, where there should be life, where there should be the pulsing of blood through this web, there is just emptiness. There's just nothing. It's not darkness so much as just the absence of energy, the absence of such such sustenance. And that that emptiness is spreading through the web, and the knots are beginning to crumble and flicker and fail and tear, and you can see cracks stretching across the land.

DM: And the veil slams down again, and the clarity you had is gone, and you're now standing on the top of the Red Mesa. It's evening, and everything is again distorted by grey, the ground itself unsteady under your feet. And it cracks open beneath you, the rock shifting as if you are traversing an unstable glacier and not solid ground, solid rock. And you can feel now here the absence of something. You can feel this is where the Heart should be. This is where the blood flows. This is where the energy that powers that web of people, that web of thought, that web of souls that protects Dunmar, is ripped loose. And the web, the energy is flapping in the wind. The connections between these people that bind Dunmar together and hold this energy is gone.
